analysis.one_liner: Extends federal anti-discrimination and equal pay protections to independent contractors.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would give independent contractors the same federal discrimination protections as employees, never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Education and Labor Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Independent contractors are not covered by the main federal laws that ban workplace discrimination based on race, sex, age, disability, or genetic information, and they are not covered by the equal pay rule. This bill would rewrite those laws so that anyone working under an independent contract is treated as an employee for those protections. It was introduced by Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton and never advanced past the committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: The millions of people who work as independent contractors — gig workers, freelancers, and contract employees — would gain the right to sue for discrimination based on race, sex, national origin, age, disability, or genetic information, and to bring equal pay claims, just as employees can. A contractor dropped by a company for a discriminatory reason would, under this bill, have a legal claim where today they have none.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends six federal laws — Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Rehabilitation Act, the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act, and the Fair Labor Standards Act — so that 'an individual who provides work for an employer under the terms of an independent contract' counts as an employee under each one.

Independent contractors are generally excluded from these statutes' definitions of 'employee,' which is why they lack the right to sue for workplace discrimination or unequal pay based on sex; the bill closes that gap by statute rather than relying on case-by-case court tests.
The CRS summary confirms the bill's single purpose: to require that independent contractors be treated as employees under these anti-discrimination and labor-standards laws.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that rely on independent contractors — from gig platforms to staffing agencies to businesses using freelancers — would face new exposure to discrimination and equal pay lawsuits, plus the recordkeeping and compliance costs that come with employee-status coverage. Some businesses might respond by hiring fewer contractors or converting them to employees.

drawbacks.text: The bill treats every independent contractor the same way. A fully independent freelancer with multiple clients is in a very different position from a worker who is economically dependent on one app or one company, but the bill would cover both, and a one-size-fits-all rule could impose costs and legal exposure on genuinely independent small businesses that hire other freelancers.

Businesses facing new liability for discrimination claims by contractors might respond by pulling work back in-house, cutting contractor roles, or requiring contractors to form formal entities to stay outside the statute — changes that could reduce contracting opportunities the law does not directly address.

The Fair Labor Standards Act amendment is limited to the equal pay provision (Section 6(d)); it does not extend minimum wage or overtime rules to contractors, so the bill is narrower on pay than a reclassification bill would be.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and targeted: contractors who face discrimination currently have no federal remedy, and this bill would give them one. The main cost is that the definition is broad — it sweeps in all independent contractors, including genuinely independent freelancers — which would raise legal risk for businesses that engage them. A more tailored bill could protect dependent contractors specifically. Weighed against that, the bill never went anywhere, so no costs or benefits were ever tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the bill on September 6, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors in the House.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote. The bill remained in committee when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that use independent contractors are better off, because they avoided the new discrimination and equal pay liability the bill would have created; the bill was introduced late in the Congress with no cosponsors and no committee action, so its backers made no progress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Contract-hiring companies, which avoided new liability

for.name: Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.role: Delegate, District of Columbia; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor

against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: 425 of 434 other House members
against.what_they_did: Declined to cosponsor the bill; it ended with zero cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: With zero cosponsors and no votes, the record shows no partisan pattern; the sponsor was a Democratic delegate and no Republican or Democratic member signed on.

industries.industry: Gig platforms and on-demand app companies
industries.note: These companies classify workers as independent contractors, which shields them from discrimination and equal pay suits. The bill would remove that shield, creating a path for contractors to sue — a cost the companies avoided when the bill died.
Firms that place independent contractors with employers would take on new exposure to discrimination claims for the workers they place, while the workers they place would gain legal rights.
Because the bill covers all independent contractors, even small businesses hiring independent freelancers would face new compliance and liability costs under the anti-discrimination laws.
